title: TypeScript essentials
intro: TypeScript adds a type system to JavaScript, helping you catch many mistakes before your code runs. In this lesson, you will learn the core TypeScript features you need to read and write practical code in modern frontend and backend projects.
takeaways: TypeScript adds static type checking to JavaScript and can catch many mistakes before your code runs.
Type annotations are useful for variables, function parameters, return values, and object structures, while inference avoids unnecessary annotations.
Union types, literal types, interfaces, and optional properties let you describe realistic application data precisely.
Narrowing with typeof, in, and equality checks helps TypeScript understand which type a value has in a particular branch.
TypeScript types disappear during compilation, so type checking does not replace runtime validation of external data.

quiz.question: What is one of the main benefits TypeScript provides during development?
options: It makes JavaScript execute without a browser
It can catch many type-related mistakes before the program runs
It automatically creates a backend server
It prevents all runtime errors
quiz.explanation: TypeScript checks your code during development and compilation, which allows many type-related mistakes to be found before the application runs. It cannot prevent every runtime error.

quiz.question: What does this TypeScript code allow?
options: let status: "todo" | "done" = "todo";
The variable can contain any string
The variable can contain either "todo" or "done"
The variable can only contain numbers
quiz.explanation: This is a union of literal types. The variable can contain exactly the string "todo" or the string "done".

quiz.question: What does the optional property marker mean in this interface?
options: interface Task { dueDate?: string; }
dueDate must always be an empty string
dueDate must be a number
dueDate is optional and may be undefined
quiz.explanation: The question mark makes the property optional. A Task does not have to contain dueDate, so code using it must account for it being undefined.

quiz.question: What does this function return when called with an empty array?
options: function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined { return items[0]; }
null
undefined
An empty array
quiz.explanation: Accessing index 0 of an empty JavaScript array produces undefined. The return type T | undefined correctly describes both possibilities.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of this code?
options: function print(value: string | number) { if (typeof value === "string") { return value.toUpperCase(); } return value.toFixed(2); }
It converts every value into a boolean
It prevents strings from being passed to the function
It narrows the union type so each branch can use the appropriate operations
quiz.explanation: The typeof check narrows value from string | number to string in the first branch. In the remaining branch, TypeScript knows it is dealing with a number.

exercise.title: Build a typed task utility
exercise.task: Create the TypeScript types and functions for a small task manager. Define `Status` as the literal union `"todo" | "in-progress" | "done"`, and define the `Task` interface with `id: number`, `title: string`, `status: Status`, and an optional `dueDate?: string`. Implement `filterByStatus(tasks: Task[], status: Status): Task[]` so it returns only tasks with the requested status, and implement `countByStatus(tasks: Task[]): Record<Status, number>` so it always returns all three status keys with zero for statuses that do not occur. Also implement the generic function `firstOrNull<T>(items: T[]): T | null`, which returns the first item or `null` for an empty array. This editor runs the code without TypeScript type-checking, so after completing the exercise, open the code in IntelliJ IDEA and intentionally make a few type mistakes to see the errors TypeScript reports.
exercise.hint: Start with `filter` for filterByStatus. For countByStatus, initialise a Record with all three Status keys at zero and increment the matching key for every task. For firstOrNull, check whether the array has an item before returning index 0.

tests.name: filterByStatus returns matching tasks
filterByStatus returns an empty array when nothing matches
countByStatus includes all status keys
countByStatus counts every task
firstOrNull returns the first item
firstOrNull returns null for an empty array
